FRAUDULENT INDUCEMENT TO CHANGE RESIDENCE FOR WORK (LABOR CODE §§ 970-972) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, summarizes California Labor Code sections 970 through 972 — the statutory scheme, found in the chapter titled "Solicitation of Employees by Misrepresentation," that prohibits inducing a person to move in order to accept work through knowingly false representations about the work, and that gives the affected person a separate civil remedy. Where a specific inducing party and jobseeker are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be used and read on its own, without any specific party named, as a general reference to what this statute says. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular advertisement, offer, or communication complies with it, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

CORE PROHIBITION — INDUCING RELOCATION BY KNOWINGLY FALSE REPRESENTATIONS
California Labor Code section 970 prohibits any person, or an agent or officer of that person, directly or indirectly, from influencing, persuading, or engaging any person to change residence — within the state, into the state from outside, or out of the state — for the purpose of working in any branch of labor, where that influence, persuasion, or engagement is accomplished through or by means of knowingly false representations. The statute names four specific subjects on which a knowingly false representation triggers the prohibition: (a) the kind, character, or existence of the work; (b) the length of time the work will last, or the compensation for it; (c) the sanitary or housing conditions relating to or surrounding the work; and (d) the existence or nonexistence of a strike, lockout, or other labor dispute pending between the proposed employer and the persons then or last performing the work. A false representation on some other subject, not covered by any of the four listed categories, is outside what this specific statutory section reaches. The representation may be spoken, written, or advertised in printed form.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "No person, or agent or officer thereof, directly or indirectly, shall influence, persuade, or engage any person to change from one place to another in this State or from any place outside to any place within the State, or from any place within the State to any place outside, for the purpose of working in any branch of labor, through or by means of knowingly false representations, whether spoken, written, or advertised in printed form, concerning either: (a) The kind, character, or existence of such work; (b) The length of time such work will last, or the compensation therefor; (c) The sanitary or housing conditions relating to or surrounding the work; (d) The existence or nonexistence of any strike, lockout, or other labor dispute affecting it and pending between the proposed employer and the persons then or last engaged in the performance of the labor for which the employee is sought."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 970 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=970.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a prohibition of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular recruiting or relocation situation. The statute requires the false representation to be "knowingly" false and to be the means by which the person was influenced, persuaded, or engaged to change residence for work; whether a specific statement was knowingly false, and whether it was actually the means of inducing a specific move, are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve. This clause quotes the operative text of a single statutory section (§ 970); the quoted text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page, retrieved with two different User-Agent strings, before being treated as verified. This clause does not address the neighboring sections of the same chapter (Labor Code §§ 973, 974, 976, 977) that impose separate, related disclosure obligations on advertisements for work during a labor dispute or on advertisements for sales/broker/agent compensation — those are different statutory provisions with their own text and are not covered here.

CRIMINAL PENALTY FOR VIOLATING SECTION 970
Labor Code section 971 makes a violation of section 970 a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than fifty dollars ($50) nor more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), or by imprisonment for not more than six months, or by both the fine and imprisonment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any person, or agent or officer thereof, who violates Section 970 is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not less than fifty dollars ($50) nor more than one thousand dollars ($1,000) or imprisonment for not more than six months or both."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 971 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=971.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a criminal penalty of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction for a violation of section 970 — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular situation, and not a statement that any specific conduct has been or would be prosecuted. Criminal enforcement of this section is a matter for public prosecutors; this document does not describe how or whether such enforcement occurs in practice. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 971); the quoted text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page, retrieved with two different User-Agent strings, before being treated as verified. This clause is not fully independent of the core-prohibition clause in this sheet, since section 971's penalty applies only to a violation of section 970, which that other clause covers — that dependency is disclosed here rather than presented as an unrelated confirmation.

SEPARATE CIVIL REMEDY — DOUBLE DAMAGES
Beyond the misdemeanor criminal exposure described in section 971, Labor Code section 972 gives the aggrieved party a separate civil remedy: any person, or agent or officer of that person, who violates any provision of section 970 is liable to the party aggrieved, in a civil action, for double damages resulting from the misrepresentations. That civil action may be brought by the aggrieved person or that person's assigns or successors in interest, and it may be brought without first establishing any criminal liability.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In addition to such criminal penalty, any person, or agent or officer thereof who violates any provision of Section 970 is liable to the party aggrieved, in a civil action, for double damages resulting from such misrepresentations. Such civil action may be brought by an aggrieved person or his assigns or successors in interest, without first establishing any criminal liability."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 972 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=972.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a private double-damages remedy of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular dispute, and not a calculation of what damages, if any, would be available in a specific case. The statutory text sets the multiplier at double (not treble or another multiple) and describes the measure only in the general terms "double damages resulting from such misrepresentations" — it does not itemize the specific categories of loss that qualify (for example, it does not use the words "moving expenses" anywhere in its text). Whether a particular cost, including the cost of moving to or away from a work location, counts as damages "resulting from" the misrepresentation in a given case is a question this document does not resolve, since answering it would require researching how courts have construed that phrase — case-law research that is outside the scope of this statute-text-only sheet. This clause quotes a single statutory section (§ 972); the quoted text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page, retrieved with two different User-Agent strings, before being treated as verified. Source-independence disclosure: this civil remedy sits in the same chapter as, and by its own text depends on, a violation of section 970 (covered in a separate clause in this sheet) — that dependency is disclosed here rather than presented as an unrelated confirmation.

CERTIFICATION
I, Jordan Lee, certify that I prepared this information sheet as a summary of California Labor Code sections 970 through 972, for informational reference only. This information sheet does not constitute legal advice, does not evaluate the lawfulness of any specific advertisement, offer, or communication, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.

Executed on September 5, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________
